title: Why open table formats exist
summary: The limits of directory-based Hive tables on object storage, what a table format adds, and how Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi compare.

blocks.text: Part IV ended with streams committing files into lake tables many times an hour. That only works if a table on object storage can be changed atomically and read consistently. For years it could not. Chapters 22 to 25 then go deep on Apache Iceberg.
21.1 The Hive table model

In the Hive model, a table is a **directory** and partitions are **subdirectories** named after column values. The Hive Metastore stores the schema and the list of partition locations; it does not track individual files. Any engine reading the table lists the partition directories and reads whatever files it finds.

blocks.title: A Hive-style table on object storage
blocks.text:
s3://lake/sales/orders/
  dt=2026-11-15/
    part-00000.parquet
    part-00001.parquet
  dt=2026-11-16/
    part-00000.parquet
    part-00001.parquet   <- still being written by a job?

Metastore: table schema + list of dt=... locations. The table is
'whatever files are in these directories right now'.
This suited HDFS, where listing was cheap and renames atomic. On object storage those assumptions fail.
21.2 What breaks on object storage

items: **Listing is slow.** Object stores are key-value systems; listing a prefix is a paginated API call (S3 returns at most 1,000 keys per request). A table with hundreds of thousands of files can spend minutes just discovering them.
**No atomic multi-file commit.** A job writing 200 files into a partition makes them visible one by one. Readers see partial results; a failed job leaves orphan files that become part of the table.

**Rename is copy plus delete.** HDFS-era committers wrote to a temporary directory and renamed it into place. On object storage that rename copies every object, takes time proportional to data size and is not atomic.
**Partitions are physical columns.** Users must filter on `dt`; filtering on `order_ts` alone scans everything. Changing the partition scheme means rewriting the table.
**Weak schema evolution.** Columns are often matched by name or position depending on file format and engine settings; renaming or reordering can silently misread old files.
**No row-level changes.** Updating one row means rewriting its whole partition, which makes CDC (chapter 17) and GDPR deletes expensive and racy.

blocks.text: Amazon S3 has offered strong read-after-write consistency since late 2020, so the old eventual-consistency problems (and workarounds such as S3Guard) are history. Listing cost, missing atomic commits and rename cost remain, and those are what table formats solve.
21.3 What a table format adds

A table format puts a **metadata layer** between engines and files. The table is no longer 'files in a directory' but 'the exact set of files listed in the current metadata version'. Changing the table means writing new files, then atomically switching to a new metadata version. Everything else follows from that idea.

blocks.caption: The table format is a specification for metadata files, not a server.

Optimistic: a writer retries if someone else committed first, after checking for conflicts

blocks.text: 21.4 Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi

Three formats emerged around the same time from different problems. **Apache Hudi** came from Uber, focused on fast upserts into the lake. **Delta Lake** came from Databricks, focused on reliable Spark pipelines. **Apache Iceberg** came from Netflix, focused on correctness and performance of very large tables across many engines.

blocks.text: All three are open and capable; differences shift with every release. Check the current documentation before relying on a feature, especially newer ones such as Iceberg format v3 (deletion vectors, a variant type, row lineage) or Delta's latest table features.
21.5 Why Iceberg became the interoperability choice

items: **Specification first.** Iceberg is defined by a written table spec independent of any engine, so many engines can implement readers and writers.
**Catalog abstraction.** The REST catalog specification gives every engine one protocol to find tables and commit, which made multi-engine access practical (chapter 24).
**Hidden partitioning and evolution.** Queries filter on real columns; layout can change without rewriting history, which matters for long-lived shared tables.

**Vendor adoption.** Snowflake, BigQuery, AWS (Athena, Glue, S3 Tables), Trino, Starburst, Dremio, Flink, DuckDB and others read and often write Iceberg; Databricks, after acquiring Tabular in 2024, supports Iceberg alongside Delta.
**Bridges.** Delta UniForm can publish Iceberg metadata for Delta tables, and Apache XTable translates metadata between formats.

blocks.text: The practical effect: data written once in Iceberg can be read by Spark for engineering, Snowflake for BI (chapter 28) and Trino or DuckDB for ad hoc work, with no copies. That is the open lakehouse (chapter 42).

blocks.title: Spark SQL: hidden partitioning versus a Hive-style column
blocks.text:
-- Iceberg: partition by a transform of a real column
CREATE TABLE lake.sales.orders (
  order_id    BIGINT,
  customer_id BIGINT,
  amount      DECIMAL(12,2),
  order_ts    TIMESTAMP
) USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(order_ts));

-- users filter on the column they understand; pruning still works
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM lake.sales.orders
WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01 00:00:00';

A table format does not remove operations work. Snapshots, small files, delete files and orphan files accumulate and must be managed (chapter 25). It turns a fragile directory into a reliable table; it does not make it maintenance-free.
21.6 What comes next

blocks.title: Use case: from Hive tables to Iceberg
blocks.text: A company runs a Hive-style lake of 400 tables queried by Spark and Trino. Nightly jobs overwrite partitions, and analysts occasionally see half-written data; a GDPR delete takes a day of partition rewrites.
items: Large tables are converted in place with Iceberg's Spark `migrate` or `add_files` procedures, which register existing Parquet files without rewriting them.
Writers switch to Iceberg commits; readers see only complete snapshots.
Deletes become row-level operations followed by compaction (chapters 23 and 25).

blocks.text: The rest of Part V builds on this foundation: chapter 22 opens the metadata tree and the commit protocol, chapter 23 covers schema and partition evolution, time travel and row-level changes, chapter 24 covers catalogs and multi-engine access, and chapter 25 covers compaction, snapshot expiry and day-two operations.

blocks.title: Make the case for a table format
blocks.text: Your lake has 150 Hive-style Parquet tables on S3, written by Spark batch jobs and one Flink streaming job, read by Trino and Snowflake. Pain points: inconsistent reads during writes, slow planning on the largest tables and expensive deletes. Write a short decision record comparing Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi for this estate, naming the deciding criteria and the risks of migrating.
hints: Which engines must read and write, and which formats do they support today?
Can tables be migrated without rewriting data?

items: A Hive table is whatever files exist at read time.
Object storage: slow listing, non-atomic rename, no multi-file commit.
Table formats track exact file sets in metadata and commit by atomic version swap.
This brings ACID, snapshots, time travel, file-level pruning, schema evolution and row-level changes.
Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi differ in metadata design and focus.
Iceberg's engine-neutral spec and REST catalog made it the interoperability choice.

blocks.q: Why do readers of a Hive-style table on S3 sometimes see half-written data?
options: S3 is eventually consistent for new objects
Files become visible one at a time and there is no atomic multi-file commit
Parquet files are written in several parts
blocks.explain: The table is defined by directory contents, so each file appears as soon as it is written. S3 has had strong read-after-write consistency since 2020, so consistency is not the cause.

blocks.q: What is the essential mechanism that gives table formats ACID commits?
options: Using HDFS instead of object storage
Renaming a temporary directory into place
Writing new files, then atomically switching to a new metadata version that lists them
blocks.explain: Readers resolve the table through metadata, so the atomic switch is the commit. Renames on object storage are copy plus delete and not atomic, which is exactly the problem formats avoid.

blocks.q: Which statement about Iceberg hidden partitioning is correct?
options: It removes the need for any file statistics
Partitions are derived by transforms of real columns, so filters on those columns prune files
Users must add a `dt` column to every query
blocks.explain: With `days(order_ts)` the engine maps a filter on `order_ts` to partitions. The Hive model is the one that forces filters on a separate `dt` column.

blocks.q: Which was originally designed with upsert-heavy, incremental pipelines as its main focus?
blocks.explain: Hudi came from Uber's need for fast upserts and incremental pulls, with record-level indexes and merge-on-read. Iceberg focused on large multi-engine tables; ORC is a file format, not a table format.
